questions.stem: Biodiversity includes diversity at three levels. Which list names them?
options: Producer, consumer and decomposer diversity
Genetic, species and ecosystem diversity
Cellular, tissue and organ diversity
Population, climate and soil diversity
questions.explanation: Biodiversity is the variety of all living things, described at the level of genes within species, species within communities, and the range of ecosystems in a region.

questions.stem: Two populations of the same snail species differ in the number of alleles for shell colour. Which level of biodiversity does this difference describe?
options: Genetic diversity
Species diversity
Ecosystem diversity
Community diversity
questions.explanation: Variation in the alleles carried by individuals of one species is genetic diversity. Species diversity compares the number and abundance of different species, and ecosystem diversity compares habitats and communities.

questions.stem: A region contains mangroves, sand dunes, salt marsh and coastal woodland. Which level of biodiversity does this variety represent?
options: Population diversity
Ecosystem diversity
Genetic diversity
Species diversity
questions.explanation: A range of distinct habitats, each with its own community and abiotic conditions, is ecosystem diversity. Species diversity would refer to the number of species within those ecosystems.

questions.stem: Which term describes all the members of one species living in the same area at the same time?
options: Ecosystem
Biosphere
Population
Community
questions.explanation: A population is a group of organisms of one species in an area. A community is all the populations of different species in an area, and an ecosystem is the community together with its abiotic environment.

questions.stem: Which is the best example of an ecosystem?
options: A rock pool with its algae, animals, water, rocks and temperature
All the crabs living in a single rock pool at low tide
All the living things found in a rock pool, but not the water or rocks
A single seaweed plant growing on a rock in the pool
questions.explanation: An ecosystem includes the community of living things together with the abiotic (non-living) components they interact with. All the crabs form a population, and all the living things without the abiotic components form a community.

questions.stem: Food web X has 40 species with many feeding links. Food web Y has 8 species with few links. A disease wipes out one herbivore species in each. Which prediction is best supported?
options: Both webs will be disrupted equally because one species was lost from each
Web X will collapse first because more species depend on each herbivore
Web X will be less disrupted because predators have other prey to switch to
Web Y will be less disrupted because there are fewer species left that could be affected
questions.explanation: In general, the higher the biodiversity of an ecosystem, the more stable it is. With many species and links, consumers in web X have alternative food sources, so the loss of one species has a smaller effect. In web Y, predators may have no other prey.

questions.stem: Which list shows classification levels from the most inclusive to the least inclusive?
options: Species, genus, family, order, class, phylum, kingdom
Kingdom, class, phylum, family, order, genus, species
Phylum, kingdom, class, order, genus, family, species
Kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species
questions.explanation: Classification is hierarchical: each kingdom contains phyla, each phylum contains classes, and so on down to genus and species. Organisms grouped at lower levels share more features and are more closely related.

questions.stem: Two organisms belong to the same order but different families. Which statement must be true?
options: They also belong to the same genus but different species
They belong to different kingdoms but the same class
They can interbreed to produce fertile offspring
They also belong to the same class, phylum and kingdom
questions.explanation: Because classification is nested, organisms in the same order must also share every higher level: class, phylum and kingdom. Being in different families means they are in different genera and species too.

questions.stem: Modern biological classification groups organisms using which evidence?
options: Their common names in English and other languages
Physical structures and similarities in molecular sequences such as DNA
Where the organisms live and what time of day or night they are most active
Their size, colour and how useful they are to humans
questions.explanation: Classification indicates relationships between organisms, based on their physical structures and on shared similarities in DNA and protein sequences. Habitat and usefulness to humans do not reflect evolutionary relationships.

questions.stem: Species P and Q look very alike, but their DNA sequences differ greatly. Species P and R look quite different, but their DNA sequences are very similar. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: No conclusion is possible, because DNA cannot show relatedness
P is more closely related to R than to Q, despite appearances
P is more closely related to Q, because body form is more reliable
Q and R must belong to the same genus as each other
questions.explanation: Similar DNA sequences indicate recent common ancestry, so P and R are likely to be closely related. Similar appearance can arise in unrelated species living in similar environments, which is why molecular evidence has led to revisions of classification.

questions.stem: In the scientific name Panthera leo (lion), what does 'Panthera' refer to?
options: The order
The genus
The species
The family
questions.explanation: Binomial nomenclature gives each species a two-part name: the genus, with a capital letter, followed by the specific epithet, in lower case. Both parts are written in italics, or underlined when handwritten.

questions.stem: Which describes the correct way to write a scientific name, such as Homo sapiens, in typed text?
options: Both parts in capitals, with only the genus italicised
Genus capitalised, species lower case, both in italics
Both parts capitalised and printed in bold type
Genus lower case, species capitalised, both underlined
questions.explanation: The genus name starts with a capital letter, the specific name is all lower case, and the whole name is italicised in print. Bold and full capitals are not the convention.

questions.stem: The lion is Panthera leo and the tiger is Panthera tigris. What does sharing the name Panthera indicate?
options: They are the same species and can produce fertile young
They live in the same habitat in the same continent
They were both first described by the same scientist
They are in the same genus and are closely related
questions.explanation: Very closely related species are placed in the same genus, so they share the first part of the scientific name. Lions and tigers are separate species, as shown by their different specific names.

questions.stem: The same bird is known by different common names in different parts of Australia and in other countries. What is the main advantage of using its scientific name?
options: Scientific names describe the colour and size of each bird
Scientific names never change once they are first given
Scientific names show the exact place a species lives
Each species has one name used by scientists worldwide
questions.explanation: An internationally agreed system gives every species a single unique name, avoiding confusion caused by common names that vary between regions and languages. Scientific names can be revised when new evidence changes our understanding.

questions.stem: New DNA evidence shows that a species placed in genus A is more closely related to the species in genus B. What is the most likely outcome?
options: Genus A and genus B are both deleted from the classification
The species is moved to genus B and its scientific name changes
The species keeps its name, because names can never be revised
The DNA evidence is rejected, because body structure always decides
questions.explanation: The internationally agreed system of nomenclature undergoes revision as new evidence appears. Reclassifying a species into another genus changes the genus part of its scientific name.

questions.stem: Key: 1a Has six legs: go to 2. 1b Has eight legs: Spider. 2a Has wings: go to 3. 2b No wings: Silverfish. 3a Wings covered in scales: Moth. 3b Wings clear: Fly. An animal has six legs and clear wings. What is it?
options: Silverfish
Spider
Fly
Moth
questions.explanation: Six legs leads to step 2, having wings leads to step 3, and clear wings identifies the fly. A moth has scaly wings, and a spider has eight legs.

questions.stem: What is the main feature of a dichotomous key?
options: Each step lists every species that lives in the area
Each step compares the DNA of two unknown organisms
Each step gives three or more options of similar features
Each step gives a choice between two contrasting features
questions.explanation: A dichotomous key divides organisms into two groups at each step, using pairs of contrasting statements, until a single organism is identified. 'Dichotomous' means dividing into two.

questions.stem: A student writes a key step: '1a Large leaves: go to 2. 1b Small leaves: go to 3.' Why is this a poor choice of features?
options: Each step of a key must give at least four choices
Leaf size is a molecular feature that needs DNA testing
'Large' and 'small' are subjective, so users may disagree
Leaves can never be used to identify plant species at all
questions.explanation: Good key features are clear, observable and measurable, such as 'leaves longer than 5 cm' or 'leaf edges toothed'. Vague terms like large and small can be interpreted differently, leading to wrong identifications.

questions.stem: What do reproductive isolating mechanisms do?
options: Prevent members of different species from producing fertile offspring
Prevent members of a single population from finding enough food during winter
Allow members of different species to share the same habitat
Allow two species to combine into a single new species
questions.explanation: Reproductive isolating mechanisms are features that stop different species from interbreeding successfully, maintaining them as separate species. They can act before or after fertilisation.

questions.stem: Two closely related frog species live in the same pond. One breeds in early spring and the other in late summer. Which isolating mechanism is this?
options: A post-zygotic mechanism causing hybrid sterility
A post-zygotic mechanism causing hybrid death
A pre-zygotic mechanism based on gamete shape
A pre-zygotic mechanism based on breeding time
questions.explanation: Breeding at different times of year (temporal isolation) prevents mating, so no zygote forms. It is pre-zygotic because it acts before fertilisation.

questions.stem: A horse and a donkey can mate and produce a mule, but mules are almost always sterile. What kind of isolating mechanism does this show?
options: Post-zygotic: the hybrid cannot produce offspring
Pre-zygotic: the parents cannot physically mate
Pre-zygotic: the parents breed at different times
Post-zygotic: the hybrid zygote dies before birth
questions.explanation: A zygote forms and the mule develops, so the barrier acts after fertilisation, making it post-zygotic. Hybrid sterility keeps horses and donkeys as separate species because genes cannot pass on through the mule.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a pre-zygotic isolating mechanism?
options: A hybrid animal that grows to adult size but produces no gametes
A hybrid plant that produces seeds which never germinate
Two bird species with different courtship songs that females ignore
A hybrid embryo that fails to develop properly and dies early in the pregnancy
questions.explanation: Different courtship songs prevent mating, so fertilisation never occurs, which is behavioural, pre-zygotic isolation. The other three all involve a hybrid zygote that has already formed, so they are post-zygotic.

questions.stem: Pollen from flowering plant species A lands on the stigma of species B, but the pollen fails to fertilise the egg because the proteins on the two cells do not match. How is this barrier classified?
options: Post-zygotic, because the hybrid seed is sterile
Pre-zygotic, because the plants flower in different seasons
Pre-zygotic, because fertilisation is prevented
Post-zygotic, because pollen reached the flower
questions.explanation: Incompatible gametes that cannot fuse prevent a zygote from forming, so the barrier is pre-zygotic (gamete isolation). Pollen reaching the flower is not fertilisation, and no hybrid seed is produced.

questions.stem: What is an adaptation?
options: A temporary change in body shape caused by the weather
Any change in the environment that affects a population
An inherited feature that helps an organism survive and reproduce
A change an organism makes during its life because it wants to survive
questions.explanation: Adaptations are inherited structural, physiological or behavioural features that increase an organism's chance of surviving and reproducing in its environment. Individuals do not develop adaptations because they need them.

questions.stem: Which is a structural adaptation?
options: A possum feeding at night and sheltering in hollows by day
A bird migrating north each autumn to warmer places
A mammal producing very concentrated urine in dry times
The thick, waxy cuticle on the leaves of a desert plant
questions.explanation: Structural adaptations are physical features of the body, such as a thick cuticle that reduces water loss. Feeding at night and migrating are behavioural adaptations, and producing concentrated urine is physiological.

questions.stem: Some desert mammals produce very concentrated urine and obtain most of their water from food and metabolism. What type of adaptation is this?
options: Physiological
Structural
Behavioural
Ecological
questions.explanation: Physiological adaptations involve how the body's processes work, such as kidney function that conserves water. A structural adaptation would be a physical feature, and a behavioural adaptation would be something the animal does.

questions.stem: On hot days a red kangaroo licks its forearms, where blood vessels lie close to the skin. As the saliva evaporates, the kangaroo cools. What type of adaptation is the licking?
options: Physiological
Biochemical
Behavioural
Structural
questions.explanation: Licking the forearms is something the animal does, so it is a behavioural adaptation. The blood vessels close to the skin of the forearms are a structural feature that makes the behaviour effective.

questions.stem: Many eucalyptus trees have leaves that hang vertically. How does this help them in a hot, dry climate?
options: Less leaf surface faces the midday sun, reducing heating and water loss
More leaf surface faces the midday sun, increasing the rate of photosynthesis
Rain runs off the leaves so water is not absorbed by the roots
Vertical leaves have no stomata, so no water is lost at all
questions.explanation: Leaves hanging edge-on to the overhead sun absorb less heat around midday, reducing leaf temperature and transpiration. They still have stomata and still photosynthesise, especially in morning and afternoon light.

questions.stem: Plants in hot, dry habitats often have sunken stomata surrounded by hairs. Why do these features reduce water loss?
options: They make the guard cells pump water back into the leaf
They increase the leaf surface area that is exposed to the dry moving air outside
They trap humid air near the stomata, lowering the vapour gradient
They block all carbon dioxide entry so photosynthesis stops
questions.explanation: Hairs and pits trap a layer of moist, still air next to the stomata, so the concentration gradient for water vapour diffusing out is smaller. Carbon dioxide can still diffuse in, so photosynthesis continues.

questions.stem: Mammals of the same type living in colder climates tend to have smaller ears and shorter limbs than those in hot climates. Which explanation is best?
options: Smaller extremities increase the surface area for losing extra heat
Cold temperatures stop the ears and limbs of each individual animal from growing
Larger ears would freeze, so each animal shrinks them during winter
Smaller extremities reduce the surface area through which heat is lost
questions.explanation: Reducing the surface area of extremities lowers heat loss, an advantage in cold climates; large ears in hot climates help lose heat. These are inherited structural adaptations, not changes an individual makes in response to cold.

questions.stem: Which is a behavioural adaptation of a desert lizard?
options: Having long legs that hold the body well away from the hot sand surface
Basking in the morning sun and sheltering in burrows at midday
Having scaly skin that reduces water loss from the body
Excreting nitrogen wastes as uric acid to save water
questions.explanation: Moving between sun and shade to control body temperature is a behaviour. Scaly skin and long legs are structural adaptations, and excreting uric acid is a physiological one.

questions.stem: A student says giraffes grew long necks because each one stretched to reach high leaves and passed this on. What is wrong with this idea?
options: Long necks reduce survival, so they cannot be an adaptation to feeding
Stretching changes the DNA of every body cell, which is then passed on
Features gained during life are not inherited; adaptations come from inherited variation
Giraffe necks are behavioural adaptations, so they cannot be inherited at all
questions.explanation: Changes acquired during an individual's life, such as stretched muscles, do not alter the DNA in gametes and are not inherited. Adaptations arise because individuals with inherited favourable variations survive and reproduce more.

questions.stem: Some Australian plants re-sprout from buds under their bark after a bushfire. What kind of adaptation is this, and what is its advantage?
options: Structural, allowing the plant to avoid all fire damage
Structural, allowing the plant to regrow quickly after fire
Behavioural, allowing the plant to move away from fire
Physiological, allowing the plant to put out the flames
questions.explanation: Buds protected beneath thick bark (epicormic buds) are a structural feature that lets plants such as many eucalypts regrow leaves soon after fire. They do not prevent damage; they allow recovery.

questions.stem: Which list correctly gives the three types of adaptation?
options: Genetic, species and ecosystem
Pre-zygotic, post-zygotic and hybrid
Biotic, abiotic and climatic
Structural, physiological and behavioural
questions.explanation: Adaptations are classified as structural (body features), physiological (body processes) and behavioural (actions). Genetic, species and ecosystem are the levels of biodiversity.

questions.stem: Two cactus-like plants from different continents both have thick stems and spines instead of leaves, but DNA shows they belong to unrelated families. What does this suggest?
options: Similar environments selected similar adaptations in unrelated groups
The plants must belong to the same genus because they look alike
Spines are behavioural adaptations that plants learn from each other
DNA evidence must be wrong because structure always shows relationship
questions.explanation: Similar selection pressures in dry habitats can produce similar structural adaptations in unrelated organisms. This is why classification uses molecular evidence as well as physical structures.

questions.stem: Some birds fly thousands of kilometres each year between breeding and feeding areas. What type of adaptation is migration?
options: Physiological
Post-zygotic
Behavioural
Structural
questions.explanation: Migration is an inherited pattern of behaviour that lets animals exploit seasonal food and breeding sites. Physiological changes such as fat storage support migration, but the movement itself is behavioural.

questions.stem: Why is it useful for ecologists to classify organisms when comparing two ecosystems?
options: It removes the need to sample organisms in the field at all
It tells them the age of each organism in the ecosystems
It lets them identify and count species consistently to compare diversity
It shows which of the ecosystems has the warmest climate and the highest rainfall
questions.explanation: Classification and identification keys let ecologists name organisms consistently, so they can count species and compare biodiversity between ecosystems. Abiotic factors such as temperature must be measured separately.
